title: Fall and Recovery: Oak Park to the Bronx, Bennington, and the Body That Stopped
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Climbing Child: Oak Park and Chicago

stops.name: Oak Park, Illinois: the only child
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and place given independently by Encyclopaedia Britannica and by Wikipedia. Coordinates are the Oak Park town centre; no birth address was located in reachable sources.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of October a daughter is born in Oak Park, Illinois, to Horace Buckingham Humphrey, a hotel man, and Julia Ellen Wells Humphrey, a pianist. They name her Doris Batcheller. She is their only child and will remain so. The family's money is uncertain and its music is not. Julia plays, and will go on playing for her daughter's classes for twenty years, first as accompanist and later as manager of the school that keeps the household fed. Horace's earnings fail more than once in that time.
suggested_refs: Marcia B. Siegel, Days on Earth: The Dance of Doris Humphrey (Yale, 1987), the standard scholarly biography

stops.name: Oak Park, Illinois: the watchword upity
stops.date_confidence: attested as a document, dated 1897 in the NYPL finding aid (citation code C91); the month is not given and the date here only orders the segment. The letter's exact wording was returned with minor variation across two fetches of the same finding aid, so the transcription is quoted with that caution.
stops.campa: Julia writes to an aunt about the toddler in the house, who is not yet two. The letter reports a plan already failing, which was to raise an unaffected little girl. What it describes instead is a child who goes up everything within reach and has one word for what she wants. Her mother predicts, half in exasperation, a runaway career on horseback in a circus ring. The word the child keeps saying, and the word Julia spells out for the aunt, is 'upity.'
stops.quote: but to bring her [Doris] up an unaffected little girl is going to be a mighty task and I think I shall fail. I am convinced she will runaway and join the circus and become a professional bareback rider or acrobat. Such an inveterate climber I never saw and her continual watchword is 'upity.'
stops.quote_source: Julia Wells Humphrey to 'Auntie May' (May Miller), 1897; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, Jerome Robbins Dance Division, New York Public Library, citation code C91
suggested_refs: The Humphrey family correspondence, Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C91

stops.name: Francis W. Parker School, Chicago: the teacher who sends her on
stops.date_confidence: attested that she attended the Francis W. Parker School and studied under Mary Wood Hinman (Wikipedia; Britannica names Hinman among her early teachers). The 1900 entry year and the 'around age eight' start of the Hinman training are reconstructions from the institutional chronology and were not independently confirmed. Coordinates are the school's historic Lincoln Park site, not pin-verified.
stops.campa: She enters the Francis W. Parker School in Lincoln Park, a Chicago building run on progressive principles: no rote drill, art and craft and movement taught as forms of thinking. A teacher's early note on her is brief and businesslike. Here she meets Mary Wood Hinman, who teaches folk and gymnastic dance rather than ballet, clog steps and country steps and Swedish gymnastics, and who will still be advising her twenty years later. Humphrey names Hinman first among her teachers ever after.
stops.quote_source: A teacher at the Francis W. Parker School, Chicago, quoted unattributed in the Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division
suggested_refs: Mary Wood Hinman's folk and gymnastic dance curriculum at the Francis W. Parker School
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673)

stops.name: Green Lake, Wisconsin: the mother's summer report
stops.date_confidence: attested that the letter was written from Green Lake, Wisconsin in 1903 (NYPL finding aid, C160). That Doris was present is inference from the letter's contents rather than a stated fact; the month is not given and the date only orders the segment. Coordinates are the Green Lake town centre.
stops.campa: The family summers at Green Lake in Wisconsin. Julia, writing to Horace, files a report on their daughter at seven or eight: improving, on the whole a good girl, hopelessly given to putting things off. The same daughter will later run a company, a school, a theatre and a household on almost no money at all, and will be known in the studio for refusing to make a dance before the idea is finished. Julia does not know any of that. She is writing to her husband about a slow child, and the letter is kept.
stops.quote: There is the making of something fine in Doris, though I am not yet quite sure what—She is improving this summer, and is, on the whole a very good girl. Her hopeless procrastination seems to be her worst fault
stops.quote_source: Julia Wells Humphrey to Horace Humphrey, from Green Lake, Wisconsin, 1903; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C160
suggested_refs: The Julia Wells Humphrey letters, Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C160

stops.name: Oak Park, Illinois: her own school at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: Britannica gives '1913 (age 18): Opened her own dance school'. That Julia managed it and played for it, and that Humphrey found the work limiting, come from the institutional chronology and family correspondence and are reconstruction. No street address survives in reachable sources; the month only orders the segment.
stops.campa: She finishes at Parker at eighteen and does not go on to college. She opens a dance school in Oak Park instead, with Julia at the piano and over the books, and it pays: society girls, ballroom and aesthetic dancing, and enough income to hold the family up when Horace's earnings fail. It also bores her. Four years of teaching other people the steps they have asked for bring her close to leaving dance altogether, and it is Hinman, her Parker teacher, who tells her where to go instead.
suggested_refs: The Oak Park studio's account books, in the family business records of the Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

segments.name: Denishawn: Eleven Years Inside Somebody Else's Idea

stops.name: Denishawn School, St. Paul Avenue, Los Angeles: the enrolment
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1917 (Wikipedia; encyclopedia.com: 'Joined the Denishawn dance school and company in Los Angeles in 1917'). The 600 St. Paul Avenue address is attested in Wikipedia's Denishawn article. Coordinates are Nominatim's fix on Saint Paul Avenue, downtown Los Angeles, correcting two earlier pins in the research pool that fell 1.6 and 2.1 km off the street. The month only orders the segment.
stops.campa: Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn have been running the Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts on St. Paul Avenue for two years when Humphrey arrives at twenty-one, sent by Hinman. The curriculum is everything at once: yoga, Delsarte, ballet barre, Oriental and Egyptian and Greek forms, philosophy, music visualization. Within a season she is in the company. She meets Charles Weidman, a Nebraskan two years younger, and Pauline Lawrence, who plays piano and will keep the books and cut the costumes for the next twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: The Denishawn School premises at 600 St. Paul Avenue, Los Angeles, established summer 1915
sources: Wikipedia, 'Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts'

stops.name: Egan Little Theatre, Los Angeles: Valse Caprice
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Britannica confirms Valse Caprice, also called Scarf Dance, as an early Denishawn work of hers but gives no premiere date; the 7 January 1920 date and the Egan Little Theatre venue come from the NYPL-derived chronology and could not be independently fetched, since direct attempts on the NYPL finding aid returned an unrelated collection record. Coordinates are an approximate downtown Los Angeles placement.
stops.campa: Valse Caprice, which everyone calls Scarf Dance, is danced for the first time at the Egan Little Theatre downtown. The scarf does the drawing and the arm supplies it. It is a Denishawn kind of piece, a solo built around a length of silk that traces in the air the curve the body has just left, made inside the house style and inside Ruth St. Denis's method of music visualization. Humphrey is three years into an eleven-year employment and is already better at the house method than the house.
suggested_refs: Denishawn programme sheets for the 1920 Los Angeles season, Jerome Robbins Dance Division, NYPL
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Potter Theatre, Santa Barbara: Bourree alone
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The premiere date and venue come from the NYPL-derived chronology alone and were not independently confirmed. The Potter Hotel and its theatre were demolished in the twentieth century, so the coordinates mark the waterfront site approximately.
stops.campa: At the Potter Hotel's theatre on the Santa Barbara waterfront she dances Bourree alone. Denishawn works the coast constantly, playing resort houses and vaudeville circuits between Los Angeles seasons, and the soloists make their new pieces in the gaps between trains. The Potter is a millionaires' hotel with a stage attached, and its audience has come out for an evening's entertainment. She gives them a solo in strict time about how a weight falls and what catches it. Nobody records what they made of it.
suggested_refs: The Potter Hotel and Potter Theatre, Santa Barbara, demolished in the twentieth century
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Spreckels Theatre, San Diego: Soaring
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the premiere. The Spreckels Theatre on Broadway is attested and was open in 1920 (Wikipedia: opened 23 August 1912), and the coordinates are Nominatim's fix on the building; the 20 September 1920 date and the co-credit to St. Denis come from the NYPL-derived chronology alone. Britannica lists Soaring among her early works without dating it.
stops.campa: Soaring premieres at the Spreckels Theatre on Broadway, co-credited to Ruth St. Denis, on a bill with Sonata Pathetique. Six dancers hold one square of silk between them and give it in turn the shape of a wind, a wave, a bell. The group is the instrument and nobody in it is the soloist, and the co-credit does not divide the work between the two women. The house opened in 1912 and is still standing. It is the first piece of hers that later companies keep dancing.
suggested_refs: The Spreckels Theatre, Broadway, San Diego, opened 1912 and still standing
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Singapore: the Burmese Yein Pwe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Asian tour is attested in general dance history but its length is contested: the NYPL-derived chronology gives departure August 1925 and return 26 November 1926, roughly fifteen months, while Wikipedia and the popular accounts say 'two years in the Orient'. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved. The 15 July 1926 date and the Singapore venue are unconfirmed; coordinates mark the central theatre district.
stops.campa: The company sails in August 1925 and spends fifteen months in Asia, playing Japan, China, Burma, India, Ceylon, Java and the Malay states. The repertory it carries is the Orient as Denishawn sells it in American theatres, and it is now being played a few miles from the courtyards and temple grounds the material was taken from, in front of audiences who live there. In Singapore, out of what the two of them have been watching along the route, Humphrey and St. Denis build a new one and call it A Burmese Yein Pwe.
suggested_refs: Denishawn's 1925-1926 Asian tour itinerary and programmes, Jerome Robbins Dance Division, NYPL
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Kobe, Japan: At the Spring
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Date, city and work all rest on the NYPL-derived chronology and were not independently confirmed. The 26 November 1926 return date is from the same source and is what contradicts the 'two years' figure repeated in general accounts of the tour. Coordinates are the Kobe city centre; no venue is identified.
stops.campa: On the closing leg, in Kobe, she makes At the Spring. The tour has been fifteen months of ships, hotels, hired stages and a repertory of temple attitudes performed to audiences who live within walking distance of actual temples. Back home it will be remembered, and repeated in print for decades afterward, as two years in the Orient, a figure the company's own dates do not support. Humphrey is thirty, has been inside Denishawn nine years, and is beginning to make dances that have nothing in them she was taught. The company reaches the United States again on the twenty-sixth of November 1926.
suggested_refs: Denishawn's Japanese engagements of autumn 1926
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Denishawn House, Stevenson Place, the Bronx: keeping the school
stops.date_confidence: attested that Denishawn House opened on Stevenson Place in the Bronx in 1927 and that Humphrey and Weidman ran much of its teaching. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ruth_st_denis.journey.json, the canonical atlas pin for this site; note that an independent Nominatim fix on Stevenson Place gives 40.8825 / -73.8945, about 4.6 km north, and the discrepancy is flagged in the report rather than resolved here. The month only orders the segment.
stops.campa: Denishawn House opens on Stevenson Place in the Bronx, a school and a residence in one building, and St. Denis and Shawn are away touring for much of the year. Humphrey and Weidman teach it, run it and fill it, with Pauline Lawrence at the piano. Left alone with a studio, Humphrey stops making dances about anything at all and starts making one about colour itself, a ballet of moving hue with no story inside it. She explains the idea to her parents by way of what she has become sick of.
stops.quote: dinky little dances decorative or character or cute ballets, that I've gone to the extreme of abstractness I guess
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her parents, summer 1927, on the origin of Color Harmony; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C267
suggested_refs: Denishawn House, Stevenson Place, the Bronx, opened 1927
sources: Wikipedia, 'Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts'
Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C267

stops.name: Westport, Connecticut: the letter that ends eleven years
stops.date_confidence: attested. The letter is dated Westport, Connecticut, June 1928 in the NYPL finding aid (C270), which prints the passage. Britannica independently attests the 1928 departure from Denishawn with Weidman and the move to New York. Coordinates are the Westport town centre; no address is given for the house she was staying in.
stops.campa: In Westport, Connecticut, in June, she writes her parents the letter that ends eleven years. Shawn wants the enterprise run as a business, with a head at the top and obedience under it. She wants the dance. The break comes that summer. She, Weidman and Lawrence go to New York with no money and no bookings, carrying a technique she has been building in the studio against everything Denishawn teaches: fall and recovery, the body giving in to gravity and catching itself, an arc between two deaths.
stops.quote: if your aim is a smooth-running organization, there must be a head to run it, and obedience from its members. Which would be all well and good for me if it were merely a business, but it happens to be that and more. More important to me than any organization, is the dance, and more important than loyalty is sincerity
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her parents, Westport, Connecticut, June 1928; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C270
suggested_refs: The June 1928 Westport letters on the Denishawn crisis, Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C270

segments.name: Humphrey-Weidman: A Company Made Out of Nothing

stops.name: Civic Repertory Theatre, West 14th Street: Water Study in silence
stops.date_confidence: the venue address, 107 West 14th Street, is attested (Wikipedia, 'Civic Repertory Theatre') and the works are attested to 1928. The exact concert date of 28 October 1928 comes from the NYPL-derived chronology and was not independently fetched. The quote is verbatim from the finding aid, which dates the letter only to 1928; the research pool's 'October 1928' was narrative context and has been dropped.
stops.campa: At Eva Le Gallienne's theatre on West 14th Street the three of them give their first concert under their own name, four months out of Denishawn. The programme holds Sarabande and Water Study. Water Study is danced in silence, with no music at all, the dancers finding a common pulse in breath and in each other's weight, a swell that gathers along a line of bodies and breaks at the end of it. So far as the New York record shows, nobody has put a dance on a stage there without music before.
stops.quote: The group is the flowering of the dance
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her parents, 1928; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C271
suggested_refs: The Civic Repertory Theatre, 107 West 14th Street, Manhattan
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C271
NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Guild Theatre, West 52nd Street: Life of the Bee
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the programme and date, from the NYPL-derived chronology. The venue has been corrected: the research pool gave 33 West 52nd Street, but the Guild Theatre stood at 245 West 52nd Street, opened 13 April 1925 for the Theatre Guild and now the August Wilson Theatre (Wikipedia). The coordinate given is the real site, about 430 m west of the pool's. The quote is verbatim from the finding aid and dated 1929, not 1928-29 as the pool had it.
stops.campa: The group's programme at the Guild Theatre on West 52nd Street adds Air on a Ground Bass, Gigue, Concerto in A Minor, Speed, and Life of the Bee, in which a hive turns on itself and the dancers move as one organism with a fatal internal logic. The date on the bill is the thirty-first of March. She is making work faster than the bookings can absorb it, and teaching by day to pay for the nights. Her parents get a letter that year about what the making is doing to her.
stops.quote: art—commonly thought to be a pastime—is after all really a disease
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her parents, 1929; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C274
suggested_refs: The Guild Theatre, 245 West 52nd Street, opened 1925, now the August Wilson Theatre
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C274
NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Chelsea, the Humphrey-Weidman school: Jose Limon at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested that Limon enrolled at the Humphrey-Weidman school. The year has been corrected to 1929 (Wikipedia, 'Jose Limon': he enrolled in 1929 after seeing a performance); the research pool and jose_limon.journey.json give 1930, and the discrepancy is flagged in the report. No street address for the Chelsea studio was found in reachable sources, so the coordinates are an approximate Chelsea placement. The quote is dated ca. 1928 in the finding aid.
stops.campa: The Humphrey-Weidman school in Chelsea takes in a Mexican painter of twenty-one who has seen one modern dance concert and given up painting for it. Jose Limon cannot dance, is too tall for it, and starts anyway. Humphrey puts into him the principle she has been building since Denishawn: weight, the fall into gravity, the recovery out of it. He stays in her orbit for twenty-nine years. Around this time she writes to her parents that she cannot manage being a person and an artist at once.
stops.quote: I am a social outcast, and it is simply impossible for me to keep up, both as a person and as an artist—maybe other people know how to do both—I don't
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her parents, ca. 1928; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C271
suggested_refs: The Humphrey-Weidman school, Chelsea, Manhattan
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C271

stops.name: Maxine Elliott's Theatre, West 39th Street: the Dance Repertory Theatre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The founding of the Dance Repertory Theatre by Humphrey, Weidman, Graham and Tamiris is widely attested in dance history, but the 5 to 9 January 1930 season dates, the venue and the list of Humphrey premieres come from the NYPL-derived chronology and were not independently confirmed. The theatre address is from general historical knowledge, not pin-verified.
stops.campa: Four choreographers who compete for the same small audience decide to pool it. Humphrey, Weidman, Martha Graham and Helen Tamiris found the Dance Repertory Theatre and open a joint season at Maxine Elliott's Theatre on West 39th Street. Humphrey brings A Salutation to the Depths, Breath of Fire, Drama of Motion, La Valse and Descent into a Dangerous Place. Drama of Motion has no music and no subject: it is movement asserting that movement is sufficient. The cooperative lasts two seasons.
suggested_refs: Maxine Elliott's Theatre, 109 West 39th Street, Manhattan
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Maxine Elliott's Theatre: The Shakers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the premiere date and venue, from the NYPL-derived chronology; the work's existence and its enduring reputation are attested across general dance-history literature, and it is among the 24 Humphrey works held in Labanotation by the Dance Notation Bureau. That the second Dance Repertory Theatre season used the same theatre is assumed from the chronology, not confirmed.
stops.campa: In the second season she gives The Shakers, also called Dance of the Chosen. The men stand on one side and the women on the other and the floor between them is not crossed. They shake, and the shaking is worship and is also everything the discipline forbids, forced out through the hands. She has read the histories and the hymns, and what she makes is not a document of a celibate American sect but a theatre piece about bodies under a rule. It is still danced, and the Dance Notation Bureau holds the score.
suggested_refs: Labanotation score of The Shakers, Dance Notation Bureau, New York
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: The S.S. Dominica, the West Indies: two things she brings home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The meeting with Charles Francis Woodford aboard the S.S. Dominica during a West Indies voyage rests on the NYPL family correspondence as relayed by the institutional chronology and was not independently confirmed. The coordinate is a notional position in the eastern Caribbean, near the island the ship was named for; the vessel's actual track is not documented in reachable sources.
stops.campa: She takes a West Indies passage aboard the S.S. Dominica, thirty-five years old and worked to the bone. Aboard she meets Charles Francis Woodford, an English merchant marine officer whom everybody calls Leo. He is at sea for a living and will stay at sea. In the islands she watches Bahamian dancing and stores it. She has told her parents she does not believe in marriage. She marries him the following year, and the Bahamian material goes onstage at the Lyric two years after that.
suggested_refs: The Humphrey family correspondence for 1931, Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Morrisville, Pennsylvania: the postscript
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage and the year: Britannica gives '1932: Married Charles Woodford', and encyclopedia.com independently gives June 1932. The exact day and the Morrisville venue come from Humphrey's own postscript as printed in the NYPL finding aid (C302), which is a primary document but was not cross-checked against a civil record. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's fix on Morrisville, Bucks County, about 900 m from the pool's.
stops.campa: She marries Woodford at Morrisville, Pennsylvania, on the tenth of June. Her parents learn of it from a postscript at the bottom of a letter about something else, four lines long and signed with a single initial. The marriage does not reorganise her life. Woodford is at sea for most of every year, the company stays where it is, and Pauline Lawrence goes on running the household accounts along with everything else. On the programmes she is Doris Humphrey, as before.
stops.quote: I forgot to mention that Doris Humphrey married Charles Francis Woodford on June 10th, 1932 in Morrisville Pennsylvania. This information to be used as you see fit. D.
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey, postscript to a letter to her parents, 1932; Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division, citation code C302
suggested_refs: The Humphrey-Woodford correspondence, Doris Humphrey Collection, NYPL
sources: Doris Humphrey Collection finding aid, NYPL (archives.nypl.org/dan/19673), C302

segments.name: Bennington and the New Dance Trilogy

stops.name: Lyric Theatre, West 42nd Street: Run Little Chillun
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for date and venue, from the NYPL-derived chronology; the Lyric address is from general historical knowledge and was not pin-verified. That Humphrey said Bahamian movement observed on the 1931 voyage informed the ritual dance is her own reported account. The evidence supports mediated authorship from borrowed observation; it does not establish a claim of sole invention by her, and no legal dispute is recorded in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Hall Johnson's Black folk opera Run Little Chillun opens at the Lyric on West 42nd Street with Humphrey's choreography. For the revival scene she uses movement she watched in the Bahamas two years before. The score, the libretto and the cast are Hall Johnson's; the dances are hers. A white choreographer stages ecstatic Black religious dance out of borrowed observation and is credited for it. She never claimed to have invented it, and no dispute over it appears in any reachable source. The production runs into the summer.
suggested_refs: Hall Johnson, Run Little Chillun, Lyric Theatre, 1933; production records in the Jerome Robbins Dance Division, NYPL
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: New York: the son, and the first Broadway credit
stops.date_confidence: attested. Britannica gives '1933: Son Charles Humphrey Woodford born' and '1933: Broadway debut with School for Husbands'. The 8 July birth date and the swift return to the stage in Suite in E come from the NYPL-derived chronology. Coordinates are the canonical New York pin; no hospital or theatre is identified for either event.
stops.campa: Charles Humphrey Woodford is born in New York on the eighth of July, carrying both his parents' names. His mother is back onstage in Suite in E within weeks, and by autumn she has her first Broadway credit under her own name, The Dream of Sganarelle for the Theatre Guild's production of The School for Husbands. The commercial work is not a detour from the concert work. It is what pays for it, along with the teaching, Lawrence's costume jobs and Weidman's Broadway engagements.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Guild's The School for Husbands, 1933, Humphrey's first Broadway choreography credit
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: New York: the father's death and Life Begins at 8:40
stops.date_confidence: the Broadway revue Life Begins at 8:40 is attested to 1934 by Britannica. Horace Humphrey's stroke in 1930 and his death on 17 March 1934 come from the NYPL family correspondence chronology and were not independently confirmed; the place is given only as Illinois, and whether Humphrey travelled for the funeral is not stated in any reachable source. The stop is placed at her own New York pin for that reason.
stops.campa: Horace Humphrey, four years after a stroke, dies in Illinois in March. Whether his daughter travels for the funeral is not recorded anywhere reachable. Julia has been living inside her daughter's company for a decade and stays there. In the autumn Humphrey choreographs Life Begins at 8:40, a Broadway revue carrying Bert Lahr and Ray Bolger, and the fee goes where every fee goes, into a company and a school whose receipts never quite meet the outgoings. The revue plays the Winter Garden.
suggested_refs: Life Begins at 8:40, Winter Garden Theatre, 1934
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Bennington College, Vermont: four who agree on nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested twice over: Wikipedia gives Humphrey on the founding faculties of the Bennington School of the Dance in 1934, and the article on Martha Hill names Humphrey, Graham, Weidman and Holm as its faculty from 1934 to 1942. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from hanya_holm.journey.json, martha_graham.journey.json and jose_limon.journey.json, the canonical atlas pin for the campus. The month only orders the segment.
stops.campa: Martha Hill puts four choreographers who agree on almost nothing onto one Vermont campus for six weeks and calls it the Bennington School of the Dance. Humphrey, Martha Graham, Charles Weidman and Hanya Holm teach side by side, each with a technique that contradicts the others, in front of students who will go home and teach it in colleges across the country. The name that groups the four of them is applied later and by other people. The school runs every summer until 1942.
suggested_refs: The Bennington School of the Dance, 1934-1942, Bennington College, Vermont

stops.name: Bennington College, Vermont: New Dance
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exact date. Bennington's centrality to her major work of the 1930s is attested (Wikipedia), but the 3 August 1935 premiere date comes from the NYPL-derived chronology and was not independently confirmed. New Dance is among the works held in Labanotation by the Dance Notation Bureau. Coordinates are the canonical atlas Bennington pin.
stops.campa: New Dance premieres at Bennington, the first part of a trilogy set to Wallingford Riegger. It is not a story. A society is built onstage out of individuals who begin apart and end inside a shared order that erases none of them, and the argument is made in weight, level and phrase rather than in mime. She describes it as the world as it ought to be. Theatre Piece and With My Red Fires, which are the world as it is, follow within the year, and the three are made to answer one another.
suggested_refs: Labanotation score of New Dance, Dance Notation Bureau, New York
sources: NYPL-derived institutional chronology (secondary compilation, not independently reverified)

stops.name: Bennington College, Vermont: the trilogy completed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1936 dating of Theatre Piece and With My Red Fires comes from the NYPL-derived chronology and general dance-history summary. That the three parts were never performed as one evening in her lifetime is unsourced in anything reachable and is recorded as unverified. That Theatre Piece is lost is supported indirectly: it is absent from the Dance Notation Bureau's 24 notated Humphrey works, which do include New Dance and With My Red Fires.
stops.campa: Theatre Piece goes at competition: a world of people fighting one another for work, for applause, for money.
